A Gentle Re-Entry

4 capstone project briefs
Hermann Ebbinghaus showed more
than a century ago that memory de-
cays exponentially without retrieval
practice. The forgetting curve is
not a metaphor; it is measured data.
The only reliable countermeasure
is spaced repetition —and a capstone
project is the most intense form of it.
You will retrieve every concept you
have learned, in context, under pres-
sure. Six months from now, what you
built will be what you remember.
Twelve weeks ago you stood at the threshold . We asked what
it means to place a language model in conversation with a corpus it
has never seen, to retrieve the right fragment at the right granularity,
and to ground the model’s response so firmly in evidence that hal-
lucination becomes the exception rather than the rule. In the weeks
since, the vocabulary grew rich: chunking strategies and semantic
boundaries, cascaded retrieval pipelines, derivative artifacts that give
your system many lenses on one truth, RAPTOR’s hierarchical sum-
maries, GraphRAG’s entity–relation webs, request-side and response-
side guardrails, query transformation, semantic caching, the structured
bridge of Text-to-SQL, and—this final week—the discipline of evalua-
tion that binds it all together. Each week planted a seed.

This document presents your capstone project options: twelve distinct
applications, each designed to integrate every pillar of the course. You
will design chunking strategies for real corpora, build cascaded retrieval
pipelines, enrich your knowledge layer with at least one advanced
technique (RAPTOR, GraphRAG, or derivative artifacts), implement
guardrails and response grounding, bridge structured and unstructured
data with Text-to-SQL, and evaluate everything with the rigor this
course demands.
Think of these twelve projects as your project of last resort: if you cannot
conceive of something better, one of these will serve you well. But we
would be delighted if you surprise us with something entirely your
own.
What Must You Carry Forward
When the capstone concludes , you should be able to:
• Architect an end-to-end RAG system from a set of ambiguous
requirements—decomposing the problem into ingestion, chunking,
retrieval, enrichment, guardrails, grounding, and evaluation deci-
sions
• Design a chunking strategy that respects the semantic boundaries
of your corpus—not arbitrary token windows, but boundaries that a
domain expert would recognize
• Build a cascaded retrieval pipeline that moves from cheap, broad
recall (BM25, keyword) through dense semantic search to expensive,
precise re-ranking—and justify every stage

• Enrich your knowledge layer with at least one advanced technique:
RAPTOR hierarchical summaries, GraphRAG entity–relation extrac-
tion, or derivative artifacts that rewrite your corpus into multiple
complementary views
• Implement guardrails on both request and response sides—catching
adversarial or off-topic queries before they reach the retriever, and
grounding every response in retrieved evidence with auditable cita-
tions
• Bridge structured and unstructured data by integrating Text-to-SQL
or structured query interfaces alongside your document retrieval, so
the system can answer questions that live in databases as naturally

• Evaluate honestly: define retrieval metrics (precision, recall, MRR),
faithfulness metrics (groundedness, citation accuracy), and end-to-
end quality metrics—then report failures as openly as successes
• Ship something that works end-to-end for at least one realistic use
case—imperfect but functional, defensible, and ready for critique
If you can do all of these, you are ready to build RAG systems that
serve real organizations with real stakes.
The Five Pillars: Cross-Cutting Requirements
Every capstone project must exercise five interdependent pillars .
No project is complete unless it demonstrates mastery of each.
Pillar 1: Retrieval Architecture
A RAG system is only as good as its retrieval .

Pillar 1: Retrieval Architecture
A RAG system is only as good as its retrieval . Your project must
demonstrate a thoughtful, multi-stage retrieval pipeline:
• Chunking: Choose a strategy appropriate to your corpus. Fixed-size
token windows are the baseline; your capstone must go beyond
them. Consider semantic chunking (split at topic boundaries), re-
cursive chunking, or document-structure-aware chunking (sections,
headings, paragraphs). Justify your choice with evidence.
• Embedding model selection : Choose an embedding model and
defend it. Compare at least two (e.g., OpenAI text-embedding-3-large

[Page 8]

vs. an open-source model like bge-large or e5-mistral-7b). Report
embedding quality on your domain.
• Hybrid search: Implement both sparse (BM 25/keyword) and dense
(vector) retrieval. Demonstrate when each wins and when the hybrid
outperforms either alone.
• Re-ranking cascade: After initial retrieval, apply a cross-encoder or
LLM-based re-ranker. Report the lift in precision from re-ranking.
Pillar 2: Knowledge Enrichment
Raw chunks are the floor , not the ceiling . Your project must
implement at least one advanced knowledge enrichment technique:
RAPTOR Build hierarchical summaries of your corpus. Leaf nodes are
chunks; parent nodes are summaries of clusters. Demonstrate that
RAPTOR retrieval answers “big picture” questions that chunk-level
retrieval misses.
GraphRAG Extract entities and relationships from your corpus and
build a knowledge graph.

GraphRAG Extract entities and relationships from your corpus and
build a knowledge graph. Show that graph-based retrieval answers
multi-hop questions (“which suppliers share a common risk factor?”)
that vector search alone cannot.
Derivative Artifacts Rewrite your corpus into complementary views:
executive summaries, glossaries, FAQ pairs, comparison tables, or
domain-specific indices. Show that querying these artifacts improves
answer quality for specific question types.
You may implement more than one. Projects that demonstrate two
or more enrichment techniques, with measured comparison, will be
recognized.
Pillar 3: Query & Response Intelligence
The space between the user ’s question and the system ’s answer is
where intelligence lives . Your project must demonstrate:
• Query transformation : At least one technique—query rewriting,
HyDE (hypothetical document embeddings), query decomposition,
or step-back prompting. Report the retrieval improvement from
transformation vs. raw query.

sponse.

Pillar 4: The Structured Bridge
Not all knowledge lives in prose . Every project has structured data
alongside its document corpus—databases, spreadsheets, APIs with
tabular responses, or metadata catalogs. Your project must:
• Identify the structured data in your domain (e.g., patient databases,
patent metadata, financial transaction logs, sensor readings).
• Implement a Text-to-SQL or structured query interface that translates
natural language questions into database queries.
• Demonstrate the router: given a user question, does the system route
to document retrieval, structured query, or both? Report routing
accuracy on a test set.
• Show at least one question that requires both structured and unstruc-
tured retrieval to answer correctly.
Pillar 5: Evaluation as Discipline
Evaluation is not a post-hoc checklist. It is embedded in the design.
You will:
• Define metrics before you build.
• Retrieval metrics: Precision@k, Recall@k, MRR, NDCG. Report on a
held-out test set of at least 50 queries.
• Faithfulness metrics : What percentage of generated claims are
grounded in retrieved evidence? Use an LLM-as-judge or NLI-based
approach. Report faithfulness score.

• End-to-end quality: Human evaluation on a sample of 20+ queries.
Use a rubric: correctness, completeness, clarity, citation quality.
• Ablation study: Remove one pillar at a time (e.g., disable re-ranking,
remove GraphRAG, turn off query transformation) and report the
quality delta. This is your evidence that each component earns its
place.
• Report both successes and failures. If your system fails on 15% of
cases, say so. Diagnose why. Failure analysis is data.
The Twelve Projects at a Glance
Each project is grounded in a real domain , with real corpora, real
stakeholders, and real consequences for getting it wrong.
1. The Legislative Cartographer Navigate overlapping zoning codes, build-
ing regulations, and environmental ordinances for urban planners.
Domain: municipal governance.
2. The Patent Prospector Prior art search across millions of patents for
IP attorneys and R&D engineers. Domain: intellectual property.
3. The Clinical Trial Matchmaker Match patients to eligible clinical trials
from ClinicalTrials.gov. Domain: healthcare and clinical research.
4. The Compliance Sentinel Monitor financial regulatory compliance across
SEC, FINRA, and Basel III requirements. Domain: banking and fi-
nance.
5. The Maintenance Oracle Surface relevant procedures from thousands
of maintenance manuals and sensor logs for aviation and industrial
equipment. Domain: aerospace and manufacturing.

10 capstone project briefs
• Corpus complexity: The domain must have at least 1,000 documents
(or equivalent volume) with non-trivial structure—not a toy dataset.
• Retrieval challenge: Simple keyword search must be demonstrably
insufficient. The corpus must reward semantic search, re-ranking, or
multi-hop retrieval.
• Enrichment requirement: At least one of RAPTOR, GraphRAG, or
derivative artifacts must be applicable and measurably beneficial.
• Structured data: The domain must include structured data (databases,
APIs, metadata catalogs) alongside the document corpus.
• Guardrails requirement: The domain must have clear failure modes
that guardrails can prevent (hallucinated citations, off-topic responses,
PII leakage, harmful advice).
• Evaluation requirement : A quantitative metric, a test set of 50+
queries, and a faithfulness benchmark.
• Feasibility: You must be able to prototype and evaluate it in 4 weeks.
Come to office hours with your proposal and a one-page design docu-
ment.

On Crystallization
When you pour hot syrup into cold
water, it crystallizes into a hard, co-
herent structure. Learning works the
same way. The capstone project is
your cold water. The concepts you
learned in Weeks 1–12 are the hot
syrup. When you apply them under
pressure, in the service of a real prob-
lem, they crystallize into permanent
knowledge.
1. Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels (HyDE).
Gao et al., 2022. Hypothetical document embeddings for query trans-
formation.
2. ColBERT: Efficient and Effective Passage Search via Contextualized
Late Interaction over BERT. Khattab & Zaharia, 2020. A re-ranking
architecture that balances quality and latency.
3. Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through
Self-Reflection. Asai et al., 2023. Teaches the model to decide when
to retrieve and whether the retrieval was useful.
4. Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Scaling and Optimiz-
ing RAG Pipelines. A survey of production RAG patterns. Good
context for architectural decisions.
5. RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Gener-
ation. Es et al., 2023. A framework for RAG evaluation metrics.
Directly applicable to Pillar 5.
6. Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial
Gender Classification. Buolamwini & Gebru, 2018. Critical for any
project involving human data. Understand fairness and the risks of
distributional bias in retrieval.

A Calibration Note
The capstone is not a competition . It is an opportunity to inte-
grate and consolidate what you have learned. We prioritize depth
over coverage. If you fully understand cascaded retrieval, knowledge
enrichment, response grounding, the structured bridge, and evaluation
discipline—even if your project covers only one use case—you have
succeeded.
We do not expect perfection. We expect honesty. A system that retrieves
the right chunk 75% of the time and says so clearly is more valuable
than one that claims 95% and hides the failure cases. Failure analysis is
data. It reveals where your assumptions broke.
Architecture and clarity matter more than heroics. A well-documented,
testable, clearly-orchestrated RAG pipeline is infinitely more valuable
than an opaque monolith that sometimes works. The capstone is
your chance to prove you can build something other engineers will
understand and extend.
We look forward to seeing what you build.

low-income clients annually—receives a housing case. The landlord
claims the apartment is uninhabitable, but the tenant has not paid
rent. The lawyer must find precedents: When does a landlord’s duty
of habitability supersede a tenant’s rent obligation? What jurisdiction
matters? What if the case is in Cook County, Illinois? Has an Illinois
appellate court ruled on this specific scenario?
Currently, the lawyer spends hours in law libraries (or on expensive
databases like Westlaw, LexisNexis) searching case law. The Open Case-
book changes this. It gives legal aid organizations, solo practitioners,
and law students free access to 6.7 million court decisions spanning 360
years—and a RAG system that finds relevant precedents in seconds,
not hours.
This capstone teaches retrieval fundamentals through the lens of real
legal practice. Case law is a perfect domain for learning dense vs.
sparse retrieval because the distinctions are stark: a case citation
(“Brown v. Board, 347 U.S. 483”) is pure keyword signal; the legal
reasoning patterns buried in opinion text require semantic understand-
ing. Matryoshka embeddings are fascinating here: at 256 dimensions,

The institutional setting is a legal aid organization or solo practice
serving low-income clients. The geography is Illinois, specifically Cook

Metrics for each query and each dimension :

The Domain
The institutional context is Doctors Without Borders / Médecins
Sans Frontières (MSF), the humanitarian medical organization operating
in 70+ countries. The geographic focus is sub-Saharan Africa and
Haiti—regions with weak health infrastructure where MSF operates
primary care clinics and emergency response.
Setting and constraints :
• Field clinics in South Sudan (Bentiu, Malakal), Haiti (Port-au-Prince
area), Democratic Republic of Congo (Kalemie), and similar.
• Staff: 1 physician, 2–3 nurses, 1–2 health workers, 0–1 lab technician.
• 300–500 patients per day (emergency, acute, chronic).
• Essential drugs: limited to 200–400 medications (WHO Essential
Medicines List).
• Lab capacity: malaria rapid test, pregnancy test, maybe blood glu-
cose; no microbiology culture, no genetic testing.

Medical challenges specific to this context :

• Pregnancy complications: High maternal mortality. Protocols for

• Limited labs: No microbiology; clinical diagnosis is the standard.

• Drug stock variability : A clinic may be out of chloroquine but

The Domain
The institutional setting is a developer tools company (inspired

Traditional RAG pipelines do this: extract text from the PDF, split it into

works beautifully for prose-heavy documents. It fails catastrophically
for documents where layout is meaning.
This capstone asks a pointed question: When should you skip text extrac-
tion entirely and retrieve document pages as images, letting a vision-language
model read them directly?
The answer is not “always.” It is not “never.” It is: it depends on the query
and the page. Your job is to build both pipelines—traditional text-chunk
RAG and vision-language page retrieval—run them side by side on the
same corpus of SEC filings, and measure where each wins. The result
is not just a working system but a decision framework for when to use
which route in production.

(10-Q), proxy statement (DEF 14A), and material event disclosures (8-K)
through EDGAR. The database contains over 21 million filings dating
back to 1993, all freely downloadable.

nies in the Dow Jones Industrial Average , covering the most recent
five fiscal years (2021–2025). This gives you 30 × 5 = 150 filings, each
60–200 pages long, totaling roughly 15,000 pages.

The Earnings Analyst is a capstone about knowing your tools .
The traditional text-chunk RAG pipeline—chunking, embedding, hy-
brid search, reranking—is the workhorse of enterprise RAG. It handles
prose beautifully. But when the document’s meaning lives in its lay-
out—in tables with merged headers, in waterfall charts, in footnoted
financial statements—text extraction is lossy, and the VLU route (page
images + vision-language models) is the honest choice.
The lesson is not “VLU is better.” The lesson is: build both, measure both,
and route intelligently. That decision framework—when to chunk text
and when to show the page—is what separates a junior RAG engineer
from a senior one.

The five capstone pillars manifest concretely in this legislative
RAG project:
1. Retrieval Architecture.
• Chunking: semantic chunking by LAMC section boundary, not by
token count. Section 12.114 (all of it) is one chunk, even if 3,000

• Embedding: augmented embeddings account for overlay relationships.
Fine-tuned on regulatory domain pairs.

2. Knowledge Enrichment (GraphRAG).
• Cross-reference extraction: every “See also section X.YZ” and “As

The five capstone pillars are realized distinctly in patent prospecting:

Architecture
The Clinical Trial Matchmaker is a four-stage system:
Stage 1: EHR Data Structuring. The patient’s EHR is semi-structured:
diagnosis, prior treatments, lab results are often free-text notes. Stage 1
parses the EHR and extracts a canonical patient profile:
• demographics: age, gender, performance _status (ECOG score).
• diagnosis: cancer _type, stage, genetic_mutations (BRAF, KRAS, NRAS, etc.),
prior_responses.
• prior_treatments: drug _list, dates, duration, response (CR/PR/SD/PD), toxicities.
• organ_function: creatinine, albumin, hemoglobin, ANC, ALC.
• comorbidities: cardiovascular, renal, hepatic, CNS metastases (size/location).
• contraindications: allergy history, intolerance notes.
This extraction uses NLP (entity recognition for drug names, lab value
extraction via regex, negation handling for negative findings). The
result is a JSON-structured patient object.
Stage 2: Trial Protocol Parsing. Clinical trial protocols (from Clinical-
Trials.gov) are semi-structured documents: inclusion criteria, exclusion
criteria, study phase, primary outcome, etc. are demarcated sections.
Stage 2 parses each trial protocol and extracts:
• trial_metadata: nct _id, title, sponsor, phase, status (recruiting/active/closed).
• location: institution, city, state (filters by geography).
• inclusion_criteria: list of criterion objects, each with condition (e.g.,
“age 18-75”), type (age/stage/mutation/prior_treatment).
• exclusion_criteria: list of criterion objects (e.g., “ECOG ≥2”, “active CNS
disease”).

Evaluation
Evaluation in clinical matching is high -stakes: false negatives
(missing eligible trials) harm patients; false positives (recommending

strategy is asymmetric: recall is paramount, but precision is also critical.
Golden Set Curation. Recruit 20 oncologists (from MD Anderson, UT

golden set of 60–100 patient-trial pairs labeled as “eligible.”

and measure: of all manually-identified eligible trials, what fraction
does the system retrieve in its top- 20 results? Target: 100% recall (no
eligible trial left unfound).

Semantic Caching (Highly Valuable Here). Compliance officers ask
similar questions repeatedly. “What capital requirements apply to
mortgage-backed securities?” is asked by the risk team, the CFO, and
external auditors—possibly dozens of times per year. Semantic caching
stores the most-frequently-queried regulations and their answers in

first: if a semantically similar query was answered in the past 90 days,
return the cached answer (with update note: “this answer was cached

rate in compliance: typically 40–60% for large banks, yielding massive
latency improvements.

The Vision
Aircraft maintenance is a search problem in disguise . A techni-
cian at Southwest Airlines or American Eagle discovers an unfamiliar
squeaking sound during a post-flight inspection, captures it in the
maintenance computer (MCC) system as a squawk 1, and now must
find the right course of action within seconds. Is this a known fault?
Has Boeing published a service bulletin? Does this symptom appear
in the Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) for our 737-800 fleet? Will
this ground the aircraft or can it fly with restrictions?
The Maintenance Oracle is a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system
that turns unstructured squawks, fault codes, and technician queries
into precise retrieval chains pointing to authoritative sources: AMMs,

The Vision
In the first 72 hours after a humanitarian crisis — earthquake,
flood, conflict, famine— information is life . A id organizations
need to answer questions in real time :
Which organizations are active in the Antakya district? Who is providing
medical care? Are there water and sanitation services in place? What is
the current population in need? Where are the gaps?
The Humanitarian Dispatch is a retrieval system built on crisis situation
reports (SitReps): concise, timely field briefs published by UN agencies,
NGOs, and government authorities during a disaster response. During
the 2023 Turkey-Syria earthquake, over 100 organizations published
500+ SitReps in the first two weeks. A coordination officer in Istan-
bul reviewing resource allocation decisions had no systematic way to
ask, “Which organizations are covering rural areas in Hatay Province?”
or “Are any sectors under-resourced in Gaziantep?” Instead, they
scrolled through email threads and PDF attachments, missing critical
information or duplicating efforts.
The Humanitarian Dispatch solves this through a multi-lingual RAG
system that indexes SitReps, structures them via GraphRAG (entity-
relation graphs of organizations, sectors, districts, and services), and
answers coordination queries with evidence chains pointing to source
reports.

The Humanitarian Dispatch addresses three architecture chal -
lenges that differ from maintenance or fact -checking systems:
1. Multi-lingual Retrieval at Scale. Turkish field reports describe needs
in Turkish; Arabic reports use Arabic. English coordination summaries
appear in OCHA documents. The system must search across all three
languages, retrieve the best match regardless of language, and translate
sub-sections on demand for a coordinator who reads only English.
Solution: A tri-lingual embedding model (e.g., mMultiBERT or fine-
tuned mBERT on humanitarian corpora) that maps all three languages
to a shared embedding space. A coordinator queries in English; the sys-
tem retrieves matching documents in Turkish and Arabic with metadata
translations.
2. Entity Explosion. SitReps mention hundreds of organizations, dis-
tricts, organizations-sector pairs, and temporal states (“as of 2023-02-
15”). A simple keyword search returns dozens of irrelevant SitReps.
The system must identify entities (organization names, sector codes,
districts) and their relationships, then filter and rank by those relation-
ships.
Solution: Named entity recognition (NER) fine-tuned on humanitarian
text, graph construction (entities as nodes, relationships as edges), and
entity-aware ranking.

The Newsroom Verifier is a fact-checking RAG system. It accepts a

dence from a knowledge graph of political statements, votes, legislative

1. Claim Decomposition as Primary Task. Before retrieval begins, the
system decomposes the claim into atomic sub-claims:
Input: "Senator Smith voted against every infrastructure bill."
Decomposition:
1. Scope: "Every" → temporal scope, geographic scope, domain scope
- Temporal: last decade? entire tenure? specific Congress?

5. Evaluation as Discipline. Fact-checking evaluation is rigorous and
multifaceted:
• Decomposition Quality: Expert annotators review 100 decomposed
claims. Are the sub-claims faithful to the original? Do they capture
the intended meaning? Metric: inter-annotator agreement ≥ 0.87.
• Retrieval Completeness: For 50 test claims, manually verify the com-
plete set of relevant bills. Does the system retrieve all of them?
Metric: Recall ≥ 0.95 (missing even one bill can lead to false ver-
dicts).
• Categorization Accuracy: Expert manually categorize 500 bills. Does
the system’s automatic categorization match? Metric: Precision
≥ 0.92, Recall ≥ 0.88.
• Verdict Correctness: For 100 claims with published fact-check verdicts
(from PolitiFact), does the system’s verdict match expert verdicts?
Metric: Agreement ≥ 0.90.
• Evidence Chain Auditability: For every verdict, can a journalist follow
the evidence chain and verify each step? Metric: 100% of verdicts
must be fully traceable to sources.
• False Negative Rate (Critical): How many false claims does the system
incorrectly rate as True? Metric: < 1% (one false verdict per 100
claims is unacceptable for journalism).

Summary
The Newsroom Verifier is RAG in service of democratic account -
ability. It combines claim decomposition, multi-hop retrieval, entity
disambiguation, temporal reasoning, and structured data lookup. The
system serves journalists who must verify facts under deadline pressure.
Every claim must be traceable; every verdict must be defensible.
Unlike the Maintenance Oracle (which tolerates rare retrieval errors
because safety protocols catch them) or the Humanitarian Dispatch
(which operates under time pressure with incomplete data), the News-
room Verifier operates in public, on record. A false verdict published
is a credibility incident that damages trust in news institutions. The
standard is not “useful” but “bulletproof.”
Building this capstone requires mastering claim decomposition (a non-
trivial NLP task), designing retrieval systems that achieve high recall
(missing evidence is worse than finding too much), and thinking deeply
about ambiguity and uncertainty. It is a powerful demonstration of
RAG’s potential to amplify human expertise in knowledge work.

Architecture
Pharmacovigilance RAG faces five distinct challenges :
1. Distinguishing Correlation from Confounding. A patient reports liver
injury while taking drug X and concomitant medications A, B, C, heavy
alcohol use, and pre-existing liver disease. Did drug X cause it? Or
is it confounding? The system must retrieve the patient’s full medical
context and flag potential confounders.
2. Temporal Reasoning (Dechallenge and Rechallenge). A patient takes
drug X, develops rash (Day 10), stops drug (Day 15), rash resolves
(Day 22). This pattern (symptom onset after drug initiation, resolution
after discontinuation) strongly suggests drug causation. Conversely, if
rash persists after drug discontinuation, causation is less likely. The
system must extract temporal events from narratives and apply dechal-
lenge/rechallenge logic.

3. Mechanistic Plausibility. A report of peripheral neuropathy in a
cancer patient on chemotherapy might be plausible (chemotherapy is
neurotoxic) or coincidental (neuropathy is common in diabetes, which
the patient might have). The system must retrieve mechanistic evidence:
Is the drug known to cause this effect? Are there in vitro or animal
studies? Is there a known metabolic pathway involved?
4. Heterogeneous Report Quality. Some FAERS reports are detailed
clinical narratives from healthcare professionals (high quality). Others
are incomplete patient self-reports (low quality). The system must
weight reports by quality and explicitly flag when signal detection
relies on low-quality data.
5. Regulatory Constraints on Language. A signal report can never claim
causation. Regulatory language requires: “A potential signal is flagged,”
“Case clustering suggests,” “Mechanistic plausibility is supported by.”
Causation requires randomized controlled trials. The system’s response
grounding must strictly adhere to this linguistic boundary.

• Never use: “Drug X causes [adverse event].” Instead: “A potential

• Always distinguish signal strength: “weak (statistical signal only),”

• Flag data quality issues: “[N] of [M] reports lack dechallenge infor-

case_id INT PRIMARY KEY,

case_narrative TEXT,
age INT, gender VARCHAR(10)

case_id INT,
drug_id INT,
drug_start_date DATE,
drug_role VARCHAR(50) -- suspect, concomitant, interacting

case_id INT,

-- Query: "Count reports of liver injury in patients on drug X in the last 6 months"
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT cr.case_id)
FROM case_reports cr
JOIN case_drugs cd ON cr.case_id = cd.case_id
JOIN case_outcomes co ON cr.case_id = co.case_id
WHERE cd.drug_id = (SELECT id FROM drugs WHERE name = 'Drug X')
AND cd.drug_role = 'suspect'
AND co.outcome_term LIKE '%hepatotoxicity%'
OR co.outcome_term LIKE '%ALT%'
AND cr.report_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '6 months'
AND cr.reporter_type = 'HCP' -- Filter for high-quality reports
ORDER BY cr.report_date DESC

5. Evaluation as Discipline. Pharmacovigilance evaluation is clinical-
grade rigorous:
• Signal Detection Sensitivity (Recall): For 50 known drug-AE pairs
with published signals, does the system detect them? Metric: Recall
≥ 0.88 (missing signals is dangerous).
• False Positive Rate (Precision): How many flagged signals are spurious
(due to confounding or random variation)? Metric: Positive Predic-
tive Value ≥ 0.70 (false alarms erode trust, but some false positives
are acceptable in early signal detection).

• Temporal Extraction Accuracy: Expert-annotated test set of 100 case
narratives with ground-truth temporal events. Does the system
correctly extract drug initiation, AE onset, and dechallenge dates?
Metric: ≥ 0.92 accuracy.
• Causality Assessment Agreement: For 50 cases, does the system’s
Naranjo score agree with expert assessment? Metric: Correlation
≥ 0.82.
• Regulatory Language Compliance: Expert review 30 signal reports. Do
they adhere to FDA/EMA language restrictions (no unwarranted
causality claims)? Metric: 100% compliance (regulatory violation is
critical failure).
• Clinical Actionability: Do signal reports produced by the system align
with actual regulatory decisions (FDA label updates, communica-
tions)? Metric: Recall of real-world regulatory actions ≥ 0.85.

What Makes This RAG Challenge Unique
Unlike typical RAG (e.g., customer support QA), the Curriculum
Weaver must:
• Handle depth heterogeneity: the same concept (gradient descent)
appears in Goodfellow at three different depths across chapters; the
system must not conflate them
• Respect pedagogical ordering: you cannot read about transformers
before understanding attention; retrieval alone is insufficient without
ordering
• Synthesize across formats: lecture videos, textbook chapters, code,
and papers have radically different structures and require different
synthesis strategies
• Learn student models: the system should infer a student’s knowl-
edge baseline from interactions and adjust retrieval accordingly (this
is adaptive RAG, not just RAG)

Chunking is conceptually driven, not size driven. Each chunk is a
complete pedagogical unit: a full definition, a worked example, or a

on textbooks and lecture notes) rather than a generic model. Embed-

(distance from “SGD” to “Adam” should be small; distance from “SGD”
to “Bayesian Networks” should be large).
Hybrid search combines BM 25 (for concept names and technical
keywords) with dense retrieval (for semantic relationships).

Pillar 3: Query & Response Intelligence
Query transformation is essential because students do not articulate
precise information needs. A query like “Explain neural networks” is
too broad; the system must infer:
• Intended depth: is the student a beginner or advanced?
• Specific focus: universal approximation? backpropagation? modern
architectures?
• Prerequisite gaps: should we start with calculus refresher, linear
algebra, or both?
The transformation can be rule-based (if query contains keyword “why,”
ask for intuition; if query contains keyword “derive,” ask for formal
proof) or LLM-based.
Response grounding requires attribution to source. When the system
synthesizes content from Goodfellow and Boyd, it must clearly indicate
which insights came from which source:
Gradient descent updates the parameter θ as follows (Goodfellow, Deep
Learning, Chapter 8): θ ← θ − η∇θ L(θ).
This approach is guaranteed to converge for convex loss functions with
appropriate step size (Boyd, Convex Optimization, Chapter 9).
Failure to ground is a serious flaw in educational RAG; students may
memorize synthetic text and miss the original authors’ nuance.
Guardrails ensure the system does not generate incorrect mathematics.
Before synthesizing, check:
• Do quoted equations appear verbatim in the source?
• Do derived equations follow logically from prior passages?
• Does the system ever claim certainty about unsettled research ques-
tions?

The Vision
Federal and large enterprise procurement is opaque. Each year,
the US federal government issues over $ 600 billion in contracts. Yet
most procurement officers lack systematic access to historical data.
When writing a new RFP for, say, software development services, an
officer might ask: “What have we paid vendors for similar work in the
past year? What were the typical contract terms? Which vendors have
we worked with, and what was their performance record?”
The Procurement Analyst solves this problem. It ingests RFP documents
(unstructured text), contract terms and history (semi-structured or struc-
tured data), and vendor performance reviews (natural language feed-
back), then synthesizes answers to competitive intelligence questions in
seconds.

The Vision
Biomedical research is drowning in papers . Each year, PubMed
indexes over 1 million new articles. For a researcher conducting a
systematic literature review on, say, immunotherapy outcomes in non-
small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), the workflow is grueling: search
PubMed, screen 5,000+ abstracts for inclusion criteria (PICO: Popu-
lation, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome), download and review
200–500 full texts, extract data, assess risk of bias, synthesize findings.
Screening alone takes weeks of expert time, and biases creep in: fatigue,
inconsistency, missed papers.
The Research Synthesizer automates this. It ingests a corpus of PubMed
papers (abstracts and full texts), encodes the inclusion criteria using
structured PICO definitions, screens papers at scale, and synthesizes
findings across the included studies. The system does not replace
human judgment (a domain expert still reviews the final set), but it
accelerates screening by 5–10x and ensures consistency.
This capstone is technically rich: GraphRAG models author-topic-
method citation networks, semantic embeddings distinguish relevant
from irrelevant papers at a granular level, and evaluation measures
screening accuracy (sensitivity, specificity) against human gold stan-
dards—metrics that matter in biomedical research.

The institutional context is a biomedical research center or aca-

center, or a pharmaceutical research organization.

A typical systematic review workflow :
1. Formulate a structured research question (PICO format):
• Population: Adults aged 18+ with diagnosis of stage IIIB–IV
non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC)
• Intervention: PD-L 1 inhibitor monotherapy (e.g., pembrolizumab,
atezolizumab, durvalumab)
• Comparison: Chemotherapy (platinum + taxane) or best support-
ive care

• Outcome: Overall survival (OS) at 1–2 years, progression-free
survival (PFS), adverse events
2. Search PubMed, Embase, Web of Science for all papers matching the
population/intervention/comparison keywords
3. Screen abstracts: apply inclusion/exclusion criteria to titles and
abstracts (automated or manual)
4. Screen full texts: for papers passing abstract screening, obtain full
text and verify against detailed inclusion criteria
5. Extract data: tabulate patient demographics, study design, interven-
tions, outcomes
6. Assess risk of bias: evaluate study quality using standardized tools
(e.g., Cochrane Risk of Bias, GRADE methodology)
7. Synthesize: perform meta-analysis (if appropriate) or narrative syn-
thesis of findings
The labor bottleneck : abstract and full-text screening. A team of
2–3 reviewers screening 5,000 abstracts manually takes 40–60 hours.
Each abstract requires 1–2 minutes to read and decide. A full-text
review of 300 papers takes another 100–150 hours (20–30 minutes per
paper).

What makes this RAG challenge unique:
• Temporal complexity: regulations have versions, effective dates,
and supersession relationships. Simple keyword retrieval fails; the
system must reason about temporal validity.
• Hierarchical applicability: a facility must follow federal baseline +
state + local rules. Determining “applicable regulations” requires
graph traversal (is this facility in a non-attainment area? does the
facility’s permit incorporate this rule?).
• Dynamic data: regulations change frequently; news of changes must
be captured and integrated into the knowledge base regularly.
• Legal risk: a missed compliance requirement can result in significant
fines (often $10,000–$50,000 per day of violation for air violations).

• Permit specificity: a facility’s air permit is a legal document that con-

The Vision
A product manager at a SaaS company asks a simple question :
“What was our churn rate for enterprise accounts last quarter?” Cur-
rently, she emails a data analyst, waits 2–4 hours, receives a CSV , loads
it in Excel, and computes the metric. If she wants to slice by region,
customer segment, or product version, she must ask again.
The Revenue Compass changes this. It accepts natural language queries,
retrieves the data warehouse schema (which tables? which columns?),
retrieves the business glossary (what does “churn” mean? logo or
revenue?), retrieves past successful queries (how have others asked
this?), and generates accurate SQL. The PM sees the answer in seconds,
can modify the query, and understands how the metric was computed.
This capstone exercises all five RAG pillars, with Text 2SQL as the
undisputed star. It is the only capstone where SQL generation is
central, not optional. Students learn:
• Retrieval Architecture: Retrieving schema documentation, metric
definitions, and past queries.
• Knowledge Enrichment: Building a schema graph (tables, columns,
relationships, business metrics, lineage).
• Query & Response Intelligence : Text-to-SQL generation, error han-
dling, and query validation.
• Structured Bridge (Text2SQL): THE STAR.

• Knowledge Enrichment: Building a schema graph (tables, columns,

Architecture
The Revenue Compass combines all five pillars .
Pillar 1: Retrieval Architecture
Hybrid retrieval for schema discovery :
• Structured search: Tables, columns, and relationships are stored in a
database. Query: “Which tables have customer data?” → SQL: SELECT
* FROM schema WHERE table_name LIKE %customer%.
• Semantic search : Embed table descriptions, column names, and
column comments. Query: “How is customer churn measured?” →
Embed, search embeddings, retrieve relevant columns.
• Lexical search: BM 25 on table names, column names, and metadata
descriptions.

Guardrails:
• SQL injection prevention : Never concatenate user input directly
into SQL. Use parameterized queries.
• Query scope limits: Prevent queries that would return millions of
rows. Large aggregations are accepted; detail queries are warned.

• Business correctness: Does the result match the business definition

Summary
The Revenue Compass is the capstone where Text2SQL is the star .
Students master all five pillars:
• Retrieval Architecture : Retrieving schema, glossaries, and past
queries.
• Knowledge Enrichment: Building schema graphs and metric lin-
eage.
• Query & Response Intelligence : Parsing ambiguous natural lan-
guage and applying guardrails.
• Structured Bridge (Text 2SQL): Generating correct, safe, efficient
SQL.
• Evaluation: Assessing both syntactic and semantic correctness, plus
business impact.
Unlike the warm-ups, this capstone requires:
• GraphRAG for schema graph
• Text 2SQL as the core technique
• Derivative artifacts (metric definitions, past queries, validation rules)
• Guardrails and row-level security
Real-world impact: After completion, the system can be deployed in
actual SaaS companies. It reduces data team burden and democratizes
analytics access. Students should consider productizing their system or
contributing to open-source data platforms (Metabase, Superset, dbt).
